questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Simplify: ¾ of 168 + 25% of 360 ÷ 6 − 8²

solution.concept: 'Of' (and a percentage of) is worked first, then ÷ and ×, then + and −
solution.explanation: ¾ of 168 = 126 and 25% of 360 = 90. Next the division: 90 ÷ 6 = 15. Then 126 + 15 − 64 = 77.
solution.why_others_wrong: 152 skips the ÷ 6 (126 + 90 − 64); −28 works left to right, dividing 126 + 90 by 6; 125 reads 8² as 2 × 8 = 16.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
6.25 × 0.48 + 0.9 ÷ 0.025 − 2.5² = ?

solution.concept: Clear the decimals: 6.25 = 25/4, and dividing by 0.025 is multiplying by 40
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.35 divides 0.9 by 0.25 instead of 0.025 (3.6); 34 squares 2.5 as 5; 45.25 adds 6.25 instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the smallest number by which 2,450 must be divided so that the quotient is a perfect square?

solution.concept: Write the number as a product of primes; divide out every prime that appears an odd number of times
solution.explanation: 2,450 = 2 × 5² × 7². Only the prime 2 has an odd power, so dividing by 2 leaves 5² × 7² = 1,225 = 35².
solution.why_others_wrong: Dividing by 5 gives 490, by 7 gives 350 and by 10 gives 245, none of which is a perfect square (5 and 7 already appear squared).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x = √5 + 2, what is the value of x − 1/x?

solution.concept: Rationalise 1/x: multiply the numerator and denominator by √5 − 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 2√5 is x + 1/x; √5 − 2 is 1/x itself; 9 + 4√5 is x².

solution.concept: Write everything as a power of 5/3: (3/5)ⁿ = (5/3)⁻ⁿ and (9/25)⁻³ = (25/9)³ = (5/3)⁶
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 takes the right side as (5/3)³; −9 takes it as (5/3)⁻⁶ (forgetting that the negative power flips 9/25); 11/3 treats (3/5)^(x − 4) as (5/3)^(x − 4), giving 3x − 5 = 6.

solution.concept: a⁰ = 1 and a⁻¹ = 1/a; keep the sign of (−1/3)⁻¹ = −3
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/2 drops the minus sign of the numerator; −3/4 takes (−1/3)⁻¹ as +3 (denominator 12); −5/3 takes (0.6)⁰ as 0 (numerator −10).

solution.concept: Square both sides before isolating x
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 forgets to square 13/12 (x/144 = 1/12); 169 is 13², the numerator before subtracting 144; 5 is √25, the square root of the answer.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the square root of 12,34,54,321?

solution.concept: Numbers made of 1s have palindromic squares: 11² = 121, 111² = 12,321, 1,111² = 12,34,321, …
solution.explanation: 12,34,54,321 rises 1-2-3-4-5 and falls back 4-3-2-1, the pattern of 11,111² (five 1s). Check: 11,111² = 12,34,54,321.
steps: Digits rise to 5 and fall back ⇒ five 1s
solution.shortcut: 1…1 (n ones) squared reads 1, 2, …, n, …, 2, 1 for n ≤ 9.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If a = 2.36 and b = 1.64, what is the value of (a³ + b³) ÷ (a² − ab + b²)?

solution.concept: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), so the quotient is simply a + b
solution.explanation: Since a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), the expression equals a + b = 2.36 + 1.64 = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.72 is a − b (the result for a³ − b³ over a² + ab + b²); 3.8704 is ab; 16 is (a + b)².

solution.concept: Square twice: (x − 1/x)² = x² + 1/x² − 2, then (x² + 1/x²)² = x⁴ + 1/x⁴ + 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 121 forgets to subtract 2 at the second squaring; 81 is simply 3⁴; 79 forgets to add 2 at the first squaring (9² − 2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

solution.concept: 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; take the sum up to 20 and subtract the sum up to 10
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,870 forgets to remove 1² to 10²; 2,364 removes 1² to 11² (506), dropping 11² as well; 2,605 averages only the first and last squares (10 × (121 + 400)/2), but squares do not rise evenly.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the largest?

solution.concept: √a − √b = (a − b)/(√a + √b); with the same a − b, the smallest denominator gives the largest value
solution.explanation: Each difference has a − b = 2, so each equals 2 ÷ (√a + √b). The denominator is smallest for √5 + √3 (about 3.97), so √5 − √3 (about 0.504) is the largest; the others are about 0.410, 0.354 and 0.317.
solution.why_others_wrong: √7 − √5, √9 − √7 and √11 − √9 have larger denominators √7 + √5, √9 + √7 and √11 + √9, so they are smaller.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If a = 2.7, b = −1.2 and c = −1.5, what is the value of (a³ + b³ + c³) ÷ abc?

solution.concept: If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc
solution.why_others_wrong: −3 slips a sign in abc (which is positive here: 2.7 × −1.2 × −1.5 = 4.86); 0 assumes the cubes also add to zero; 1 assumes a³ + b³ + c³ = abc.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the roots of I and II and choose the relation between x and y that holds for every pair.
I. x² − 3x − 54 = 0
II. y² + 13y + 42 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise; a root shared by both equations makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: (x − 9)(x + 6) = 0, so x = 9 or −6. II: (y + 6)(y + 7) = 0, so y = −6 or −7. The smallest x (−6) equals the largest y (−6), and every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for the pair x = y = −6; x < y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both quadratics and state how x compares with y.
I. x² − 17x + 72 = 0
II. y² − 21y + 110 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise each equation; compare the largest x with the smallest y
solution.explanation: I: (x − 8)(x − 9) = 0, so x = 8 or 9. II: (y − 10)(y − 11) = 0, so y = 10 or 11. The largest x (9) is below the smallest y (10), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y reverse the comparison; every x is smaller than every y.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each equation has one positive and one negative root. Find them and decide which relation between x and y, if any, always holds.
I. x² + 2x − 63 = 0
II. y² − 4y − 45 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When the roots interleave, no single relation holds for every pair
solution.explanation: I: (x + 9)(x − 7) = 0, so x = 7 or −9. II: (y − 9)(y + 5) = 0, so y = 9 or −5. x = 7 is less than y = 9 but greater than y = −5, so no relation holds for every pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for 7 and 9; x ≤ y fails for 7 and −5; x < y and x ≥ y fail similarly.
solution.final_answer: Option B: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

Solve the two equations, whose roots are negative, and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 3x² + 20x + 32 = 0
II. 2y² + 9y + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Split the middle term: 20x = 12x + 8x and 9y = 4y + 5y
solution.explanation: I: 3x² + 12x + 8x + 32 = (3x + 8)(x + 4) = 0, so x = −8/3 ≈ −2.67 or −4. II: 2y² + 4y + 5y + 10 = (y + 2)(2y + 5) = 0, so y = −2 or −2.5. The largest x (−2.67) is below the smallest y (−2.5), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y compare 8/3 and 4 with 2 and 2.5 without the minus signs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The roots of both equations below are positive. Solve them and mark the relation between x and y.
I. 5x² − 18x + 9 = 0
II. 20y² − 17y + 3 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise by splitting the middle term; watch for a common root
solution.explanation: I: 5x² − 15x − 3x + 9 = (5x − 3)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 3 or 0.6. II: 20y² − 12y − 5y + 3 = (5y − 3)(4y − 1) = 0, so y = 0.6 or 0.25. The smallest x (0.6) equals the largest y (0.6), and all other pairs have x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for the common root 0.6; x < y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find all the roots of I and II and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 2x² + 11x + 12 = 0
II. 2y² + 19y + 45 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise both; with negative roots, the larger number is the one nearer zero
solution.explanation: I: (2x + 3)(x + 4) = 0, so x = −1.5 or −4. II: (2y + 9)(y + 5) = 0, so y = −4.5 or −5. The smallest x (−4) is greater than the largest y (−4.5), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y treat −4 as smaller than −4.5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
In equation I, k is a constant, and x = 4 is known to be one root of I. Find the other root of I and the roots of II, then choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 9x + k = 0
II. y² − 10y + 21 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: The two roots of x² − 9x + k = 0 add up to 9
solution.explanation: Sum of the roots of I = 9, so the other root is 9 − 4 = 5 (and k = 20). II: (y − 3)(y − 7) = 0, so y = 3 or 7. x = 4 is greater than 3 but less than 7, so no relation holds for every pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = 4, y = 3; x ≥ y fails for x = 5, y = 7; x > y and x ≤ y fail for the same pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option C: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Both equations have fractional coefficients. Clear the fractions, solve, and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x²/2 − 3x + 4 = 0
II. y²/2 − 9y/2 + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Multiply each equation by 2 first
solution.explanation: I × 2: x² − 6x + 8 = 0, so x = 2 or 4. II × 2: y² − 9y + 20 = 0, so y = 4 or 5. x = y = 4 is possible and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = y = 4; x ≥ y holds only for that one pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I contains |x|, the absolute value of x. Find every real x and y and choose the relation between them.
I. x² − 4|x| + 3 = 0
II. y² + 8y + 15 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Since x² = |x|², equation I is a quadratic in |x|; each positive |x| gives two values of x
solution.explanation: I: |x|² − 4|x| + 3 = 0, so |x| = 1 or 3, giving x = −3, −1, 1, 3. II: (y + 3)(y + 5) = 0, so y = −3 or −5. The smallest x (−3) equals the largest y (−3), and every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y misses the negative roots of I (x = −3 = y); x ≤ y holds only for that pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three ropes 84 m, 126 m and 210 m long are to be cut into pieces of equal length, with no rope left over. The pieces are to be as long as possible. How many pieces will there be in all?

solution.concept: The longest equal piece that divides every rope is the HCF of the lengths
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 and 30 use 21 m or 14 m pieces, which are common divisors but not the greatest; 42 is the piece length, not the number of pieces.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the largest three-digit number that leaves a remainder of 5 when divided by each of 12, 18 and 21?

solution.concept: Such numbers are 5 more than a multiple of LCM(12, 18, 21)
solution.explanation: LCM(12, 18, 21) = 252. Multiples of 252 below 1,000: 252, 504, 756. The largest required number is 756 + 5 = 761.
solution.why_others_wrong: 756 forgets to add the remainder; 1,013 (1,008 + 5) has four digits; 751 subtracts 5 instead of adding it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When a number n is divided by 6, the remainder is 4. What is the remainder when n² + 3n is divided by 6?

solution.concept: Replace n by its remainder: n² + 3n leaves the same remainder as 4² + 3 × 4
solution.explanation: n = 6k + 4, so n² + 3n leaves the same remainder as 16 + 12 = 28 when divided by 6. 28 = 4 × 6 + 4, so the remainder is 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 uses 16 + 3 (forgetting to multiply 3 by n); 0 assumes n² + 3n = n(n + 3) must be a multiple of 6, but 4 × 7 = 28 is not; 5 treats 3n as 3 + n (16 + 7 = 23 leaves 5).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the sum of all the factors (divisors) of 360, including 1 and 360?

solution.concept: For n = 2ᵃ × 3ᵇ × 5ᶜ, the sum of divisors is (1 + 2 + … + 2ᵃ)(1 + 3 + … + 3ᵇ)(1 + 5 + … + 5ᶜ)
solution.why_others_wrong: 810 leaves out 360 itself; 24 is the number of divisors, not their sum; 1,080 is three times 360, not a divisor sum.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The LCM of two numbers is 48 times their HCF, and the sum of their HCF and LCM is 1,029. If one of the numbers is 63, what is the other?

solution.concept: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
solution.explanation: HCF + 48 × HCF = 49 × HCF = 1,029, so HCF = 21 and LCM = 1,008. The other number = 21 × 1,008 ÷ 63 = 336. Check: HCF(63, 336) = 21 and LCM(63, 336) = 1,008.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,008 is the LCM, not the second number; 16 is 1,008 ÷ 63, which forgets to multiply by the HCF; 48 is the ratio LCM ÷ HCF.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the highest power of 12 that divides 40! (the product 1 × 2 × 3 × … × 40) exactly?

solution.concept: 12 = 2² × 3: count the 2s and the 3s in 40! and see which runs out first
solution.explanation: Number of 2s in 40! = 20 + 10 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 38, enough for 19 copies of 2². Number of 3s = 13 + 4 + 1 = 18. Each 12 needs one 3, so only 18 copies of 12 divide 40!.
solution.why_others_wrong: 19 counts only the pairs of 2s; 3 counts only the multiples of 12 up to 40; 38 counts the single 2s.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What are the last two digits of 7¹⁰⁰?

solution.concept: 7⁴ = 2,401 ends in 01, and any power of a number ending in 01 also ends in 01
solution.explanation: 7⁴ = 2,401, which ends in 01. 7¹⁰⁰ = (7⁴)²⁵, and numbers ending in 01 multiply to numbers ending in 01, so 7¹⁰⁰ ends in 01.
solution.shortcut: The last two digits of powers of 7 repeat in the cycle 07, 49, 43, 01; 100 is a multiple of 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 49, 43 and 07 are the last two digits of 7², 7³ and 7¹; 100 is a multiple of 4, so the cycle ends at 01.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A batter scored 110 runs, including 3 sixes and 8 fours. What percentage of his runs did he make by running between the wickets?

solution.concept: Runs from boundaries = 6 × sixes + 4 × fours; the rest came from running
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 5/11% is the boundary share; 60% divides the running runs by 100 instead of 110; 40% subtracts the 50 boundary runs from 100 and divides by 100.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Fresh grapes contain 80% water by weight, while raisins made from them contain 10% water. How many kilograms of raisins can be made from 45 kg of fresh grapes?

solution.concept: Drying removes only water: the solid part stays the same
solution.explanation: Solid in the grapes = 20% of 45 = 9 kg. In the raisins this 9 kg is 90% of the weight, so the raisins weigh 9 ÷ 0.9 = 10 kg.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 kg is the solid alone, ignoring the 10% water left in the raisins; 4.5 kg is 10% of 45; 11.25 kg divides 9 by 0.8, mixing up the two water percentages.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Meena spends 80% of her income and saves the rest. Her income rises by 15%, but she keeps her savings the same in rupees. By what percentage does her expenditure rise?

solution.concept: All the extra income goes into expenditure; compare that extra with the old expenditure
solution.explanation: Take income = 100: expenditure 80, savings 20. New income = 115 and savings stay 20, so expenditure = 95. Rise = 15 on 80 = 18.75%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15% assumes expenditure grows at the same rate as income; 75% divides the extra 15 by the savings (20) instead of the expenditure (80); 12% takes 80% of the 15% rise in income.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A refrigerator's price includes 18% GST on its pre-tax price. The GST rate is cut to 12% while the pre-tax price does not change. By what percentage does the price paid by the buyer fall (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Final price ∝ (1 + GST rate); compare 1.12 with 1.18
solution.explanation: With a pre-tax price of 100, the buyer paid 118 and now pays 112. The fall is 6 on 118 = 5.08%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.00% is the cut in percentage points of tax, not the change in price; 5.36% divides 6 by the new price 112; 33.33% is the fall in the tax rate itself (6 on 18).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a village, the number of men rose by 8% and the number of women by 12% over a year, and the total population rose by 9.6%. What was the ratio of men to women at the start of the year?

solution.concept: The overall rate is a weighted average of the two rates; use alligation
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 3 reverses the alligation; 1 : 1 would give 10%; 4 : 3 would give about 9.71%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. What is the largest angle?

solution.concept: The three angles add up to 180°
solution.explanation: 2 + 3 + 7 = 12 parts = 180°, so one part = 15°. Largest angle = 7 × 15° = 105°.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30° and 45° are the other two angles; 70° takes one part as 10°.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The monthly salaries of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 7. If each gets an increment of ₹4,000, the ratio becomes 7 : 9. What is A's present salary?

solution.concept: Let the salaries be 5k and 7k; the increment is added to both
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹14,000 is B's present salary (or A's new salary); ₹8,000 is 4k; ₹18,000 is B's new salary.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x : y = 3 : 4, what is (4x² − y²) : (x² + y²)?

solution.concept: Put x = 3k and y = 4k; k² cancels
solution.explanation: 4x² − y² = 4 × 9k² − 16k² = 20k² and x² + y² = 9k² + 16k² = 25k². Ratio = 20 : 25 = 4 : 5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 : 7 uses x and y without squaring (4 × 3 − 4 : 3 + 4); 4 : 25 takes 4x² − y² as (2x − y)² = 4k²; 5 : 4 inverts the answer.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of a mother and her daughter are in the ratio 9 : 2, and the mother is 28 years older than the daughter. After how many years will the mother be exactly three times as old as the daughter?

solution.concept: The age gap (7 parts) is fixed at 28 years
solution.explanation: 7 parts = 28 years, so 1 part = 4: mother 36, daughter 8. In n years: 36 + n = 3(8 + n) ⇒ 36 + n = 24 + 3n ⇒ n = 6. Check: 42 = 3 × 14.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 years is one part (k); 8 years is the daughter's present age; 12 years gives 48 and 20, a ratio of 2.4.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹4,200 is shared among 3 men, 4 women and 6 children so that each man gets twice as much as each woman, and each woman gets 1½ times as much as each child. How much does each child get?

solution.concept: Express every share in terms of one child's share c: woman = 1.5c, man = 3c
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹300 and ₹600 are a woman's and a man's shares; ₹323.08 divides 4,200 by the 13 people as if all shares were equal.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 2, x, y and 54 are in continued proportion, what is the value of x + y?

solution.concept: In continued proportion each term is the previous one times the same ratio r: 2, 2r, 2r², 2r³
solution.why_others_wrong: 56 adds the end terms 2 and 54; 18 is y alone; 36 takes x and y as 9 and 27 (the ratio 3 applied from 3 instead of from 2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Four years ago, the ages of A and B were in the ratio 5 : 4. The ratio of A's age four years from now to B's age four years ago is 3 : 2. What is the sum of their present ages?

solution.concept: Let A − 4 = 5k and B − 4 = 4k; then A + 4 = 5k + 8
solution.explanation: (5k + 8) ÷ 4k = 3/2 ⇒ 10k + 16 = 12k ⇒ k = 8. So A = 44 and B = 36, and the sum is 80 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 72 years is the sum four years ago; 88 years is the sum four years from now; 44 years uses A's present age instead of his age four years from now in the second ratio ((5k + 4)/4k = 3/2 gives k = 4).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The monthly cost of running a delivery van is partly fixed and partly proportional to the distance driven. It costs ₹5,600 in a month in which the van covers 600 km and ₹7,700 in a month in which it covers 900 km. What will it cost in a month in which it covers 1,200 km?

solution.concept: The extra cost of the extra distance gives the cost per km; the rest is the fixed part
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹11,200 treats the whole cost as proportional to distance (5,600 × 2); ₹10,500 is 7,700 × 1,200/900, the same mistake from the other month; ₹8,400 forgets the fixed part.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A is 3 years older than B, and B is 5 years older than C. The sum of the present ages of A, B and C is 61 years. How old is A?

solution.concept: Write every age in terms of C's age
solution.explanation: C = c, B = c + 5, A = c + 8. Then 3c + 13 = 61, so c = 16 and A = 24 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 years is B's age; 16 years is C's age; 26 years adds 3 and 5 to B instead of to C.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A man's present age is 125% of what it was 10 years ago, and 83⅓% of what it will be 10 years from now. What is his present age?

solution.concept: 125% = 5/4 and 83⅓% = 5/6; either condition gives the age, and the other checks it
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 years is his age 10 years ago; 60 years is his age 10 years from now; 45 years satisfies neither condition.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of three sisters are in arithmetic progression (equal gaps). The sum of their ages is 39 years and the product of the youngest and the eldest sisters' ages is 153. What is the eldest sister's age?

solution.concept: Let the ages be m − d, m, m + d; the sum fixes m
solution.explanation: 3m = 39 ⇒ m = 13. Then (13 − d)(13 + d) = 169 − d² = 153 ⇒ d = 4. The ages are 9, 13 and 17, so the eldest is 17.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13 years is the middle sister; 9 years is the youngest; 21 years takes d = 8 (from 169 − 153 = 16 without the square root).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When Ravi reaches his father's present age, his father will be three times as old as Ravi is now. Ravi's father is 40 years old now. How old is Ravi now?

solution.concept: Ravi reaches 40 after (40 − r) years; the father ages by the same amount
solution.explanation: If Ravi is r now, he reaches 40 after 40 − r years, when his father will be 40 + (40 − r) = 80 − r. So 80 − r = 3r ⇒ r = 20.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 years subtracts the gap from the father's age instead of adding it (40 − r = 3r); 13⅓ years uses the father's present age (40 = 3r); 60 years is the father's age at that future time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the average of the squares of the first ten natural numbers (1², 2², …, 10²)?

solution.why_others_wrong: 30.25 squares the average of 1 to 10 (5.5²); 35 divides 385 by 11; 55 is the sum of 1 to 10, not of squares.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of 8 numbers is 25. The average of the smallest three of them is 18 and the average of the largest three is 33. What is the average of the remaining two numbers?

solution.concept: Total of all = 8 × average; subtract the totals of the two groups of three
solution.explanation: Total = 8 × 25 = 200. Smallest three = 54 and largest three = 99. Remaining two = 200 − 54 − 99 = 47, so their average is 23.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 assumes the middle numbers share the overall average; 74.5 subtracts the two averages (18 and 33) instead of the two totals; 47 is the total of the two numbers, not their average.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a course, the final score is a weighted average of the theory mark (weight 70%) and the practical mark (weight 30%). A student scored 64 in theory and got a final score of 70. What did she score in the practical?

solution.concept: Final = 0.7 × theory + 0.3 × practical
solution.explanation: 0.7 × 64 = 44.8. So 0.3 × practical = 70 − 44.8 = 25.2 and the practical mark = 25.2 ÷ 0.3 = 84.
solution.why_others_wrong: 76 treats the two parts as equally weighted (2 × 70 − 64); 74 is the simple average of 64 and 84; 90 gives a final score of 71.8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bowler had conceded an average of 12.4 runs per wicket. In his next match he took 5 wickets for 26 runs, and his average fell by 0.4. How many wickets had he taken before this match?

solution.concept: Runs = average × wickets; write the new average as total runs ÷ total wickets
solution.why_others_wrong: 90 counts the wickets after the match (85 + 5); 80 subtracts the 5 new wickets; 150 forgets the 26 runs of the new match (12.4w = 12w + 60).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader sells a table at a loss of 10%. Had he sold it for ₹90 more, he would have gained 5%. What is the cost price of the table?

solution.concept: The ₹90 bridges a 10% loss and a 5% gain, i.e. 15% of the cost
solution.explanation: From 90% of the cost to 105% of the cost is 15%. So 15% of CP = ₹90 and CP = 90 ÷ 0.15 = ₹600.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹900 takes ₹90 as 10% of the cost; ₹1,800 takes it as 5%; ₹540 is the selling price at a 10% loss.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper marks a television at ₹22,500, which is 25% above its cost price. What is the cost price?

solution.concept: Marked price = 125% of cost, so cost = marked price ÷ 1.25
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹16,875 takes 25% off the marked price; ₹18,750 divides by 1.2; ₹17,500 subtracts a flat ₹5,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A workshop has fixed costs of ₹60,000 a month. Each chair costs ₹400 in materials and labour and sells for ₹700. How many chairs must it make and sell in a month to earn a profit of ₹30,000?

solution.concept: Each chair contributes SP − variable cost towards the fixed cost and the profit
solution.explanation: Each chair contributes 700 − 400 = ₹300. Needed: 60,000 + 30,000 = ₹90,000, so 90,000 ÷ 300 = 300 chairs.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 only covers the fixed cost (break-even); 100 covers only the profit; 129 divides 90,000 by the full price of ₹700.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The cost prices of two articles are in the ratio 2 : 3. The first is sold at a profit of 20% and the second at a profit of 10%, and the total profit is ₹420. What is the total cost price of the two articles?

solution.concept: Write the costs as 2k and 3k; profit = 0.2 × 2k + 0.1 × 3k
solution.explanation: Profit = 0.4k + 0.3k = 0.7k = 420, so k = 600. Total cost = 5k = ₹3,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,800 divides 420 by a simple average profit of 15%; ₹2,100 assumes 20% on the whole; ₹4,200 assumes 10% on the whole.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A dealer sells a machine at 25% above his cost, with payment due 6 months later. Money is worth 10% per annum simple interest. What is his true profit percentage, measured in today's money (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Bring the future payment to today: present worth = amount ÷ (1 + rate × time)
solution.explanation: Take cost = 100. He receives 125 after 6 months; its present worth = 125 ÷ (1 + 0.10 × ½) = 125 ÷ 1.05 = 119.05. True profit = 19.05%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25.00% ignores the delay in payment; 20.00% subtracts the 5% interest from 25% instead of dividing; 13.64% discounts for a full year instead of six months (125 ÷ 1.1).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper marks a lamp 40% above its cost price. He allows a discount of ₹168 and still makes a profit of 12%. What is the cost price of the lamp?

solution.concept: The discount equals the gap between the marked price (140% of cost) and the selling price (112% of cost)
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,400 takes ₹168 as 12% of the cost; ₹840 is the marked price; ₹672 is the selling price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shop sells socks at a fixed price per pair but runs an offer: 'Buy one pair at full price and get the second pair at half price.' What single discount on two pairs is this offer equal to?

solution.concept: Compare what is paid for two pairs with their full price
solution.explanation: For two pairs worth 2 units, the buyer pays 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 units. Discount = 0.5 on 2 = 25%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50% is the discount on the second pair alone; 33⅓% divides the saving by the amount paid (0.5 ÷ 1.5); 20% is the 'buy 4, get 1 free' equivalent.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The cost price and the marked price of an article are in the ratio 2 : 3. The shopkeeper sells it at a discount, and his discount percentage equals his profit percentage. What is the discount percentage?

solution.concept: Let CP = 2 and MP = 3; then SP = 3(1 − d) = 2(1 + d)
solution.explanation: 3(1 − d) = 2(1 + d) ⇒ 3 − 3d = 2 + 2d ⇒ d = 1/5 = 20%. Check: SP = 2.4, a 20% discount on 3 and a 20% profit on 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33⅓% is the discount that brings MP down to CP (no profit); 50% is the mark-up over cost; 25% gives SP = 2.25, a 12.5% profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi borrows ₹8,000 at 9% per annum simple interest and at once lends the same sum at 12% per annum simple interest. What is his gain over 2 years?

solution.concept: Gain per year = sum × (difference in rates)
solution.explanation: He earns 12% and pays 9%, so he gains 3% of 8,000 = ₹240 a year, or ₹480 in 2 years.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹240 is the gain for one year only; ₹1,920 is the interest he receives; ₹1,440 is the interest he pays.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹5,000 is lent at 8% per annum simple interest and ₹4,000 at 12% per annum simple interest, both on the same day. After how many years will the two amounts be equal?

solution.concept: The smaller sum grows ₹80 a year faster; it must close a gap of ₹1,000
solution.explanation: Yearly interest: 8% of 5,000 = ₹400; 12% of 4,000 = ₹480. The gap of ₹1,000 closes at ₹80 a year, so it takes 1,000 ÷ 80 = 12½ years (both amounts are then ₹10,000).
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 years leaves amounts of ₹9,000 and ₹8,800; 25 years doubles the answer; 12 years leaves ₹9,800 and ₹9,760.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper can sell a machine for ₹35,000 in cash today, or for ₹40,710 payable 18 months from now. Money earns 10% per annum simple interest. Which offer is better for him, and by how much in today's money?

solution.concept: Compare present worths: present worth = amount ÷ (1 + rate × time)
solution.explanation: Present worth of ₹40,710 due in 1.5 years = 40,710 ÷ (1 + 0.10 × 1.5) = 40,710 ÷ 1.15 = ₹35,400. That is ₹400 more than the ₹35,000 cash price, so the credit offer is better by ₹400.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'The cash offer' gets the direction wrong; ₹460 compares the amounts 18 months from now (40,710 − 40,250), not today; ₹5,710 ignores interest altogether.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The credit offer, by ₹400

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Asha invests ₹50,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded annually. Bina invests ₹50,000 for 2 years at 11% per annum simple interest. Who earns more interest, and by how much?

solution.concept: CI for 2 years = P[(1 + r)² − 1]; SI = P × r × t
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Asha, by ₹500' gets the direction wrong; ₹1,000 compares 11% SI with 10% SI; 'Asha, by ₹10,500' quotes her interest, not the difference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On ₹20,000 for 1 year at 10% per annum, by how much does the compound interest compounded half-yearly exceed the simple interest?

solution.concept: Half-yearly: rate 5% per half-year for 2 half-years
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹0 treats yearly compounding as half-yearly (for 1 year annual CI equals SI); ₹100 doubles the excess; ₹2,050 is the CI itself.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On a certain sum, the simple interest for 3 years is ₹3,000, and the compound interest (compounded annually, at the same rate) for the third year alone is ₹1,210. What is the sum?

solution.concept: SI for one year = P × r; the CI for the third year = P × r × (1 + r)²
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹12,100 divides the third-year interest by the rate; ₹1,000 is one year's simple interest; ₹11,000 is the amount after one year.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: P and Q invest in a business in the ratio 5 : 7 for the same period. Q gives 10% of his share of the year's profit to charity, and this amounts to ₹2,100. What was the total profit?

solution.concept: Q's share = 7/12 of the profit; 10% of Q's share = ₹2,100
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹21,000 is Q's share only; ₹50,400 takes Q's share as 5/12 of the profit; ₹25,200 is 21,000 × 6/5, mixing the ratio terms.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A invests ₹20,000 for 9 months and B invests ₹15,000 for 12 months in a business. Out of a profit of ₹13,200, what is A's share?

solution.concept: Profit is shared in the ratio of capital × time
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹7,543 shares by capital only (4 : 3); ₹5,657 is B's share on that wrong ratio; ₹4,400 shares by time only ₹4,400 gives A only one-third of the profit, as if B's capital-months were twice A's.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B invest in a business for the same period. A's capital is ₹5,000 more than B's, and they share the profit in the ratio 3 : 2. What is B's capital?

solution.concept: With equal periods, capitals are in the ratio of the profits
solution.explanation: A : B = 3 : 2, so the difference of 1 part = ₹5,000. B's capital = 2 parts = ₹10,000 (A has ₹15,000).
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹15,000 is A's capital; ₹5,000 is one part; ₹7,500 takes the difference as 2/3 of B's capital.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A starts a business with ₹40,000 and B with ₹50,000. After 3 months A withdraws 25% of his capital, and 6 months after that he adds ₹20,000. B keeps his capital unchanged. Out of a profit of ₹56,000 at the end of the year, what is A's share?

solution.concept: Add capital × months over the three periods for A
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹24,889 uses the starting capitals only (4 : 5); ₹32,000 is B's share; ₹28,000 splits the profit equally.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B invest ₹60,000 and ₹40,000 in a shop. C joins as a working partner without capital and receives 20% of the profit for running the shop; the rest is shared between A and B in the ratio of their capitals. If B receives ₹9,600 less than A, what is the total profit?

solution.concept: A gets 60% of the remaining 80%, B gets 40% of it
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹48,000 is the profit after C's 20%; ₹12,000 is C's share; ₹75,000 forgets C's share and takes 0.128P as the difference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A starts a business with ₹45,000. After 4 months B joins with ₹30,000. Two months after B joins, A withdraws one-third of his capital and C joins with ₹60,000. Out of a profit of ₹1,40,000 at the end of the year, what is C's share?

solution.concept: Track each partner's capital month by month: A changes after 6 months
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹44,211 ignores A's withdrawal (A = 5,40,000); ₹32,000 is B's share; ₹60,000 is A's share (15/35 of ₹1,40,000).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many litres of a 20% salt solution must be mixed with a 50% salt solution to make 60 litres of a 30% solution?

solution.concept: Alligation: (50 − 30) : (30 − 20) gives the ratio of the 20% and 50% solutions
solution.explanation: 20% : 50% = (50 − 30) : (30 − 20) = 20 : 10 = 2 : 1. So the 20% solution is 2/3 of 60 = 40 litres. Check: 8 + 10 = 18 litres of salt = 30% of 60.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 litres is the 50% solution; 30 litres splits equally; 36 litres is 60% of the total.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A 20-litre can is full of pure milk. 5 litres are taken out and replaced with water, and this is repeated. After how many such operations will the milk first fall below half of the can?

solution.concept: After each operation the milk is multiplied by (1 − 5/20) = 3/4
solution.explanation: Milk fraction after n operations = (3/4)ⁿ: 0.75, 0.5625, 0.4219, … It first falls below 0.5 after the third operation (milk = 20 × 27/64 ≈ 8.44 litres).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 leaves 11.25 litres of milk, still above 10; 4 and 5 are later than the first time it drops below half.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A vessel contains milk and water in the ratio 7 : 2. When 9 litres of the mixture are taken out and replaced with water, the ratio becomes 7 : 5. How many litres of mixture did the vessel hold?

solution.concept: Removing mixture keeps the 7 : 2 ratio; only the added 9 litres of water change it
solution.explanation: If the vessel holds T litres, after removing 9 litres it has 7(T − 9)/9 milk and 2(T − 9)/9 water; adding 9 litres of water: 7(T − 9)/9 : 2(T − 9)/9 + 9 = 7 : 5. So 5 × 7(T − 9)/9 = 7 × 2(T − 9)/9 + 63, i.e. 21(T − 9)/9 = 63, T − 9 = 27, T = 36.
solution.why_others_wrong: 27 litres is what remains after removal; 45 and 54 litres give 7 : 4.6 and 7 : 4.25, not 7 : 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Gold is 19 times as heavy as water and copper is 9 times as heavy as water. In what ratio must gold and copper be mixed to get an alloy 15 times as heavy as water?

solution.concept: Alligation on the relative weights (19 and 9) with mean 15
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 3 reverses the alligation; 4 : 6 is the same reversed ratio unreduced; 5 : 3 gives (95 + 27) ÷ 8 = 15.25.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A grocer mixes 26 kg of rice costing ₹20 per kg with 30 kg costing ₹36 per kg, and sells the mixture at ₹30 per kg. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Find the cost of the whole mixture, then compare with its selling price
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.14% takes the cost per kg as the simple average ₹28; 4.76% divides the profit by the selling price; 6.67% uses the simple average cost ₹28 and divides the ₹2 profit by the selling price ₹30.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Vessel A holds 40 litres of milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1, and vessel B holds 30 litres of milk and water in the ratio 1 : 1. 10 litres are poured from A into B and mixed well, and then 10 litres are poured from B back into A. What is the ratio of milk to water in A now?

solution.concept: Track milk and water separately; a poured quantity carries its vessel's current ratio
solution.explanation: A keeps 30 L (22.5 milk, 7.5 water). B becomes 40 L: 15 + 7.5 = 22.5 milk and 15 + 2.5 = 17.5 water. 10 L of B carries 5.625 milk and 4.375 water back to A. A: 28.125 milk, 11.875 water = 225 : 95 = 45 : 19.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 1 is A's original ratio; 9 : 7 is B's ratio after the first pour; 11 : 5 returns 10 L of B's original 1 : 1 mixture (27.5 : 12.5), ignoring what A poured into B.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Solutions with 10%, 20% and 40% acid are mixed to make 60 litres of a 25% acid solution. Equal volumes of the 10% and the 20% solutions are used. How many litres of the 40% solution are used?

solution.concept: Let a litres each of the 10% and 20% solutions and b litres of the 40%; write the volume and the acid equations
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 litres is the amount of each weaker solution; 20 litres splits the 60 litres equally; 30 litres treats the 10% and 20% as one 15% solution mixed with the 40% solution 1 : 1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A vessel is full of a mixture of milk and water. One-fifth of the mixture is taken out and replaced with water, after which milk and water are in the ratio 2 : 1. What was the ratio of milk to water at first?

solution.concept: Removing a fifth of the mixture leaves four-fifths of each liquid; then water is added
solution.explanation: Take the vessel as 1 unit with m milk and w water (m + w = 1). After the replacement: milk 0.8m, water 0.8w + 0.2. 0.8m = 2(0.8w + 0.2) and m = 1 − w give 0.8 − 0.8w = 1.6w + 0.4 ⇒ w = 1/6, m = 5/6. Ratio 5 : 1.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 : 2 and 3 : 1 give final ratios 4 : 3.6 and 2.4 : 1.6, not 2 : 1; 2 : 1 is the final ratio, not the starting one.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 12 men complete one-third of a job in 8 days. How many more men must join them so that the rest of the job is finished in the next 8 days?

solution.concept: In equal time, the number of men needed is proportional to the work left
solution.explanation: The rest is 2/3 of the job, twice the work done. To do twice the work in the same 8 days needs 24 men, so 12 more men must join.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 is the total number of men needed, not the extra men; 6 halves instead of doubling; 8 takes 2/3 of 12 men.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: 3 men or 5 women can finish a job in 12 days. A man is paid ₹600 a day, and wages are in proportion to the work done. What is a woman's daily wage?

solution.concept: 3 men do as much as 5 women, so 1 woman does 3/5 of a man's daily work
solution.explanation: 3 men = 5 women in work, so a woman's daily work (and wage) is 3/5 of a man's: 3/5 × 600 = ₹360.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,000 uses 5/3 instead of 3/5; ₹200 divides 600 by 3; ₹120 divides 600 by 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A and B together can finish a job in 12 days. A works alone for 4 days, and then B works alone for 18 days and completes the job. In how many days can B alone finish it?

solution.concept: Pair 4 days of A with 4 days of B as 4 days of joint work
solution.explanation: Think of it as A and B together for 4 days (4/12 = 1/3 of the job) plus B alone for 14 more days. So 14 days of B = 2/3 of the job, and B alone needs 14 × 3/2 = 21 days.
steps: 4 days of A + 4 days of B = 1/3 of the job
solution.why_others_wrong: 28 days is A's time alone; 18 days is B's working time here, not B's time for the whole job; 24 days doubles the joint time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A can finish a job in 8 hours and B in 12 hours. They start together at 9:00 AM, but A leaves at 11:00 AM. At what time does B finish the job?

solution.concept: Find the work done together in the first 2 hours; B does the rest alone
solution.explanation: Together they do 1/8 + 1/12 = 5/24 per hour; in 2 hours, 5/12. B does the remaining 7/12 at 1/12 per hour, taking 7 hours: 11:00 AM + 7 h = 6:00 PM.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1:48 PM assumes both work throughout (24/5 h from 9 AM); 2:00 PM is 5 hours after 9 AM; 8:00 PM has B working 9 hours.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A mason can build a wall in 10 days, and a wrecker can knock the same wall down in 15 days. They work on alternate days, the mason starting on day 1. On which day is the wall first completed?

solution.concept: Each 2-day cycle adds 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30 of the wall, but the last mason's day finishes it before the wrecker returns
solution.explanation: After 2k days, k/30 of the wall stands. On day 2k + 1 the mason adds 1/10, so the wall is complete when k/30 + 1/10 ≥ 1, i.e. k ≥ 27. So it is completed on day 2 × 27 + 1 = 55.
solution.why_others_wrong: Day 60 divides the whole wall by the 2-day net (30 cycles) and ignores the final mason day; day 30 counts cycles, not days; day 59 adds two extra cycles.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Tap A fills a 450-litre tank in 15 minutes. Tap B delivers 20 litres per minute. If both taps are opened on the empty tank, how long will it take to fill?

solution.concept: Convert both taps to litres per minute and add
solution.explanation: A delivers 450 ÷ 15 = 30 L/min; with B the total is 50 L/min. Time = 450 ÷ 50 = 9 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 22.5 minutes is B alone; 15 minutes is A alone; 37.5 minutes adds the two times.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipes A, B and C can fill a tank in 4, 6 and 12 hours respectively. A is opened on the empty tank at 8:00 AM, B at 9:00 AM and C at 10:00 AM. At what time will the tank be full?

solution.concept: Add up what has been filled by 10:00 AM, then use the combined rate of all three
solution.explanation: By 10 AM: A has run 2 hours (1/2) and B 1 hour (1/6), so 2/3 is full. All three together fill 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/2 per hour, so the last 1/3 takes 2/3 hour = 40 minutes. Full at 10:40 AM.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10:00 AM assumes the tank is full when C opens; 11:00 AM adds an hour for the last third; 10:20 AM uses the rate of A and B only for 1/6 of the tank.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two inlet pipes can fill a tank in 30 minutes and 45 minutes. A leak at the bottom drains 6 litres per minute. With both pipes open and the leak working, the empty tank fills in 36 minutes. What is the capacity of the tank?

solution.concept: Inlet rate − leak rate = 1/36 of the tank per minute; find the leak's share
solution.explanation: The inlets fill 1/30 + 1/45 = 1/18 of the tank per minute. Net rate = 1/36, so the leak removes 1/18 − 1/36 = 1/36 of the tank per minute = 6 litres. Capacity = 6 × 36 = 216 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 108 litres takes the leak as 1/18 of the tank; 270 litres uses 45 minutes in place of 36; 180 litres uses 30 minutes.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Pipe B takes 5 hours longer than pipe A to fill a tank. Together they fill it in 6 hours. How long does pipe A alone take?

solution.concept: 1/x + 1/(x + 5) = 1/6 leads to a quadratic in x
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 hours is pipe B; 12 hours is twice the joint time, true only for two equal pipes; 5 hours is the difference between the two pipes' times.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A car covers 300 km in 5 hours. A train runs 25% faster than the car. How long will the train take to cover 450 km?

solution.concept: Car speed = distance ÷ time; train speed = 1.25 × car speed
solution.explanation: Car speed = 300 ÷ 5 = 60 km/h. Train speed = 1.25 × 60 = 75 km/h. Time for 450 km = 450 ÷ 75 = 6 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.5 hours uses the car's speed; 10 hours makes the train 25% slower; 4.8 hours is 6 × 0.8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two runners start together from the same point on a 1.2 km circular track and run in the same direction at 9 km/h and 15 km/h. After how many minutes will the faster runner first catch up with the slower one?

solution.concept: To meet again, the faster runner must gain one full lap at the relative speed
solution.explanation: Relative speed = 15 − 9 = 6 km/h. Gaining 1.2 km takes 1.2 ÷ 6 = 0.2 hour = 12 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 minutes uses the sum of the speeds (opposite directions); 8 minutes is one lap at 9 km/h; 4.8 minutes is one lap at 15 km/h.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A walks from town P to town Q in 4 hours and B walks from Q to P in 6 hours. If they start at the same time, after how long will they meet?

solution.concept: Take the distance as 1: A covers 1/4 and B covers 1/6 of it per hour
solution.explanation: Together they close 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12 of the distance per hour, so they meet after 12/5 hours = 2 hours 24 minutes.
steps: Combined = 5/12 of the distance per hour
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 hours averages the two times; 2 hours halves A's time; 3 hours halves B's time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A is twice as fast as B, and B is three times as fast as C. On the same route, C takes 1 hour 40 minutes longer than A. How long does C take?

solution.concept: Time is inversely proportional to speed: if A takes t, B takes 2t and C takes 6t
solution.explanation: Speeds A : B : C = 6 : 3 : 1, so times are t : 2t : 6t. C − A = 5t = 100 minutes ⇒ t = 20 minutes. C takes 6 × 20 = 120 minutes = 2 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 hour 40 minutes is the difference itself; 20 minutes is A's time; 40 minutes is B's time.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In a 1 km race, A beats B by 100 m, and in another 1 km race B beats C by 100 m. Running at the same speeds, by how many metres would A beat C in a 1 km race?

solution.concept: Speeds are in the ratio of distances covered in the same time
solution.explanation: When A runs 1,000 m, B runs 900 m. When B runs 1,000 m, C runs 900 m, so when B runs 900 m, C runs 810 m. Hence when A finishes, C has run 810 m and A wins by 190 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 m simply adds the two margins; 100 m assumes the margins do not combine; 180 m takes 90% of 200 m.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three cyclists start together from the same point on a 1,200 m circular track and ride in the same direction at 3 m/s, 5 m/s and 7 m/s. After how many seconds will all three be together at the starting point for the first time?

solution.concept: Each returns to the start after 1,200 ÷ speed seconds; find the LCM of these times
solution.explanation: Lap times: 400 s, 240 s and 1,200/7 s. As multiples of 1/7 s these are 2,800, 1,680 and 1,200, whose LCM is 8,400; so all three are first together at the start after 8,400/7 = 1,200 seconds, having done 3, 5 and 7 laps.
solution.shortcut: In 1,200 s a rider at v m/s covers 1,200v m = v laps, a whole number for every integer speed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,400 seconds is the second meeting at the start; 8,400 seconds is a later common time; 600 seconds is when the two faster riders first meet anywhere on the track, not at the start.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat covers 12 km upstream in 48 minutes. The stream flows at 3 km/h. What is the speed of the boat in still water?

solution.concept: Upstream speed = boat speed − stream speed
solution.explanation: Upstream speed = 12 ÷ 0.8 h = 15 km/h. Boat speed = 15 + 3 = 18 km/h.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 km/h is the upstream speed; 12 km/h subtracts the stream again; 21 km/h is the downstream speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The speed of a boat in still water is five times the speed of the stream. The boat takes 3 hours longer to cover 72 km upstream than to cover 72 km downstream. What is the speed of the boat in still water?

solution.concept: With stream speed s, the boat moves at 4s upstream and 6s downstream
solution.explanation: 72/(4s) − 72/(6s) = 18/s − 12/s = 6/s = 3, so s = 2 km/h and the boat's speed is 5 × 2 = 10 km/h. Check: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 h upstream, 72 ÷ 12 = 6 h downstream.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 km/h is the stream; 12 km/h is the downstream speed; 8 km/h is the upstream speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A boat leaves point A and goes downstream. At the same moment a log is dropped into the river at A and floats with the current. When the boat reaches point B 2 hours later, the log is 24 km behind it. What is the speed of the boat in still water?

options.text: Cannot be found without the stream's speed

solution.concept: The log moves with the water, so the gap between boat and log grows at the boat's still-water speed
solution.explanation: Boat speed = b + s and log speed = s, so the gap grows at b km/h. In 2 hours the gap is 2b = 24 km, so b = 12 km/h. The stream's speed cancels out.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 km/h ignores the 2 hours; 6 km/h divides by 4; the stream's speed is not needed because it cancels in the gap.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two boats start at the same time from points A and B, 60 km apart on a river, and move towards each other. A is upstream of B. Each boat has a speed of 15 km/h in still water. They meet 36 km from A. What is the speed of the stream?

solution.concept: Their closing speed is (15 + s) + (15 − s) = 30 km/h whatever the stream
solution.explanation: They meet after 60 ÷ 30 = 2 hours. The boat from A goes downstream: 2(15 + s) = 36 ⇒ s = 3 km/h. Check: the boat from B covers 2 × 12 = 24 km.
steps: Closing speed = 30 km/h ⇒ meet after 2 h
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 km/h is the difference between the two boats' ground speeds; 12 km/h and 18 km/h are the ground speeds of the boats from B and A.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A train passes a signal pole in 10 seconds and a 160 m long platform in 18 seconds. What is its speed?

solution.concept: The extra 8 seconds are spent covering the 160 m platform
solution.explanation: The platform's 160 m takes 18 − 10 = 8 extra seconds, so the speed is 20 m/s = 20 × 18/5 = 72 km/h (the train is 200 m long).
solution.why_others_wrong: 32 km/h divides 160 m by the full 18 seconds; 20 km/h forgets to convert from m/s; 57.6 km/h converts 16 m/s.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A goods train leaves a station at 6:00 AM at 60 km/h. An express train leaves the same station at 8:00 AM on a parallel track in the same direction at 80 km/h. How far from the station will the express train draw level with the goods train?

solution.concept: The goods train's 2-hour head start is closed at the relative speed of 20 km/h
solution.explanation: Head start = 60 × 2 = 120 km. Closing speed = 80 − 60 = 20 km/h, so it takes 6 hours. The express covers 80 × 6 = 480 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 km is the head start; 360 km is how far the goods train runs in the 6 hours after 8 AM; 240 km uses the sum of the speeds.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: On parallel tracks, a 150 m train runs at 72 km/h behind a 250 m train running at 54 km/h in the same direction. At a certain moment the front of the faster train is 100 m behind the rear of the slower one. How long after that moment will the faster train have completely passed the slower one?

solution.concept: To pass completely, the faster train must gain the gap plus both lengths
solution.explanation: Gain needed = 100 + 150 + 250 = 500 m. Relative speed = 72 − 54 = 18 km/h = 5 m/s. Time = 500 ÷ 5 = 100 seconds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 seconds ignores the 100 m gap; 20 seconds covers only the gap; 14.3 seconds uses the sum of the speeds (35 m/s), as if the trains were moving towards each other.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 36 cm. What is its area?

solution.concept: Area of an equilateral triangle = (√3/4) × side²
solution.why_others_wrong: 72√3 cm² uses √3/2 instead of √3/4; 144 cm² is the area of a square of side 12; 18√3 cm² takes half the correct value.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A rectangular water tank measures 2.5 m × 1.6 m × 1.2 m on the inside. How many litres of water can it hold? (1 m³ = 1,000 litres)

solution.concept: Volume = length × breadth × height; then convert m³ to litres
solution.why_others_wrong: 480 and 48,000 litres slip a zero in the conversion; 5.3 adds the three dimensions.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cone and a cylinder have the same base radius and the same volume. The cone is 18 cm high. How high is the cylinder?

solution.concept: Cone volume = ⅓πr²h; cylinder volume = πr²H
solution.explanation: ⅓πr² × 18 = πr²H ⇒ H = 18 ÷ 3 = 6 cm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 54 cm multiplies by 3 instead of dividing; 9 cm halves the height; 18 cm forgets the ⅓ in the cone formula.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A wire bent into a square encloses an area of 484 cm². The same wire is bent into a circle. What area does the circle enclose? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: The length of the wire (the perimeter) stays the same
solution.explanation: Side = √484 = 22 cm, so the wire is 88 cm long. 2πr = 88 ⇒ r = 14 cm. Area = 22/7 × 14² = 616 cm².
solution.why_others_wrong: 484 cm² assumes the area is unchanged; 1,232 cm² doubles the correct area; 154 cm² takes the radius as 7 cm (half of 14).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A conical tent has a base radius of 21 m and a height of 20 m. It is made of canvas 2.2 m wide. What length of canvas is needed, ignoring wastage? (Use π = 22/7.)

solution.concept: Canvas area = curved surface area = πrl, where l = √(r² + h²)
solution.explanation: Slant height l = √(21² + 20²) = √841 = 29 m. Curved surface = 22/7 × 21 × 29 = 1,914 m². Length = 1,914 ÷ 2.2 = 870 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 600 m uses the height (20 m) in place of the slant height; 1,914 m is the area, not the length; 630 m divides the base area (1,386 m²) by 2.2 instead of the curved surface.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers is a multiple of 4?

solution.concept: List the sums 4, 8 and 12 and count the outcomes
solution.explanation: Sum 4: 3 outcomes; sum 8: 5 outcomes; sum 12: 1 outcome. Total 9 of 36, so the probability is 9/36 = 1/4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/3 is the probability of a multiple of 3; 1/6 counts sums 4 and 8 but forgets one outcome each; 5/36 counts only the sum 8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Fifty cards are numbered 1 to 50. One card is drawn at random. What is the probability that its number is a perfect square or a multiple of 7?

solution.concept: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); 49 is both a square and a multiple of 7
solution.explanation: Squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49 (7 numbers). Multiples of 7: 7, 14, …, 49 (7 numbers). 49 is counted twice, so there are 7 + 7 − 1 = 13 favourable cards: 13/50.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7/25 (14/50) counts 49 twice; 7/50 counts only one of the two kinds; 6/25 (12/50) subtracts the common number 49 twice.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bag contains 4 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. Three balls are drawn at random together. What is the probability that they are all of different colours?

solution.concept: Favourable = 4 × 3 × 2 choices (one of each colour); total = C(9, 3)
solution.explanation: Ways to pick one of each colour = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. Ways to pick any 3 balls = C(9, 3) = 84. Probability = 24/84 = 2/7.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/21 divides 24 by the ordered count 9 × 8 × 7 = 504; 24/729 treats the draws as with replacement and unordered; 1/3 assumes each colour is equally likely.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Four cards are drawn together at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that all four belong to the same suit?

solution.concept: Choose the suit (4 ways), then 4 of its 13 cards; divide by C(52, 4)
solution.shortcut: The first card fixes the suit: 12/51 × 11/50 × 10/49.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11/4165 is for one named suit (forgets the 4 choices); 1/256 is (1/4)⁴, treating the draws as independent for one named suit; 1/64 is (1/4)³, ignoring that the deck shrinks.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A fair die is rolled three times. What is the probability that the three numbers come up in strictly increasing order (for example 2, 3, 6)?

solution.concept: Any 3 different numbers can appear in exactly one increasing order
solution.explanation: Choose 3 different numbers from 6: C(6, 3) = 20 ways; each gives exactly one increasing sequence. Total outcomes = 6³ = 216. Probability = 20/216 = 5/54.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7/27 (56/216) also counts non-decreasing sequences with repeats; 1/6 is 1/3! as if all numbers were always different; 5/9 (120/216) counts all sequences of three different numbers.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: At a meeting, each of 12 people shakes hands once with every other person. How many handshakes take place?

solution.concept: Each handshake is a selection of 2 people from 12
solution.explanation: Number of handshakes = C(12, 2) = 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66.
solution.why_others_wrong: 132 counts each handshake twice (ordered pairs); 144 is 12²; 78 is C(13, 2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can 6 different books be arranged on a shelf so that one particular book is always at one of the two ends?

solution.concept: Place the particular book first (2 choices), then arrange the other 5
solution.explanation: The particular book can go at the left end or the right end: 2 ways. The other 5 books fill the remaining places in 5! = 120 ways. Total = 2 × 120 = 240.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 fixes the book at one end only; 720 ignores the condition; 480 counts 4 × 5!.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An examination paper has 6 questions in Part A and 4 in Part B. A candidate must answer 5 questions, with at least 2 from each part. In how many ways can the candidate choose the questions?

solution.concept: The split must be 2 + 3 or 3 + 2; add the two cases
solution.why_others_wrong: 252 = C(10, 5) ignores the condition; 120 and 60 are the two cases taken separately.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many three-digit numbers with all digits different can be formed from the digits 1 to 9 so that the number is divisible by 5?

solution.concept: Without 0, a multiple of 5 must end in 5
solution.explanation: The units digit must be 5 (no 0 is available). The hundreds and tens digits are chosen in order from the other 8 digits: 8 × 7 = 56.
solution.why_others_wrong: 64 allows the two leading digits to repeat (8 × 8); 112 also counts 0 as a units digit; 72 is 9 × 8, letting 5 appear twice.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In how many ways can 8 identical sweets be shared among 3 children so that every child gets at least one sweet?

solution.concept: Give each child one sweet first, then share the remaining 5 freely; or place 2 dividers in the 7 gaps between 8 sweets
solution.explanation: Line up the 8 sweets: there are 7 gaps between them. Choosing 2 gaps for dividers splits the sweets into 3 non-empty groups, so the number of ways = C(7, 2) = 21.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 = C(10, 2) allows a child to get nothing; 56 = C(8, 3) chooses 3 dividers; 28 = C(8, 2) uses 8 gaps.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many KCC applications did the Nandgaon branch sanction?

solution.concept: Sanctioned = applications × sanction percentage
solution.explanation: Nandgaon: 84% of 350 = 294.
solution.why_others_wrong: 56 is the number not sanctioned; 266 uses Karanpur's 76%; 140 is Nandgaon's average loan in ₹ thousand.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many KCC applications did the five branches receive in all?

solution.concept: Add the 'applications received' column
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,750 is the number sanctioned; 2,050 leaves out Nandgaon; 2,500 is an addition slip of 100.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which branch sanctioned the largest total amount of KCC loans in 2025-26?

solution.concept: Total amount = number sanctioned × average loan
solution.explanation: Totals (₹ thousand): Rampur 360 × 120 = 43,200; Sitapur 390 × 110 = 42,900; Nandgaon 294 × 140 = 41,160; Bhimpur 364 × 125 = 45,500; Karanpur 342 × 105 = 35,910. Bhimpur is the largest (₹4.55 crore).
solution.why_others_wrong: Sitapur sanctioned the most applications but has a smaller average loan; Nandgaon has the largest average loan but the fewest sanctions; Rampur is second at ₹43,200 thousand.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking the five branches together, what percentage of the KCC applications received were sanctioned (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Overall rate = total sanctioned ÷ total received; do not average the five percentages
solution.why_others_wrong: 74.00% is the simple average of the five percentages, which ignores the different numbers of applications; 70.00% divides by 2,500; 27.08% is the share not sanctioned.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many litres of diesel did Van R use in the week?

solution.concept: Litres used = distance ÷ mileage
solution.explanation: Van R: 1,600 km ÷ 20 km per litre = 80 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 85 litres is Van S; 32,000 multiplies distance by mileage; 75 litres is Van Q.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What total distance did the five vans drive in the week?

solution.concept: Add the distance column
solution.why_others_wrong: 5,140 km leaves out Van S; 6,060 km is an addition slip of 100; 4,560 km leaves out Van R.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the fleet's overall mileage for the week, i.e. total distance ÷ total diesel used (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Overall mileage is not the simple average of the five mileages
solution.explanation: Diesel used: 70 + 75 + 80 + 85 + 55 = 365 litres. Overall mileage = 6,160 ÷ 365 = 16.88 km per litre.
steps: Litres: P 70, Q 75, R 80, S 85, T 55
solution.why_others_wrong: 17.20 is the simple average of the five mileages; 16.00 divides by 385 litres (an addition slip); 16.50 averages only the lowest and highest mileages (12 and 21).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If Van S had been replaced by a van giving 17 km per litre, covering the same distance, how many litres of diesel would have been saved in the week?

solution.concept: Litres = distance ÷ mileage, before and after
solution.explanation: Van S used 1,020 ÷ 12 = 85 litres. At 17 km per litre it would use 1,020 ÷ 17 = 60 litres. Saving = 25 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 litres is the new consumption, not the saving; 5 litres is the gain in mileage (17 − 12); 2,550 is the saving in rupees (25 × 102), not litres.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many bales arrived in December 2025, January 2026 and February 2026 together?

solution.concept: Add the three bars (each in thousands)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,25,000 adds November to January; 1,96,000 uses March in place of February; 1,65,000 is the total for January to March.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage were the arrivals in November 2025 more than those in October 2025 (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Percentage increase = increase ÷ earlier value × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 38.24% divides by November's 68; 161.90% is November as a percentage of October; 26.00% is the increase in thousands, not a percentage.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average number of bales arriving per month over the six months?

solution.concept: Average = total of the six bars ÷ 6
solution.explanation: Total = 42 + 68 + 85 + 72 + 54 + 39 = 360 thousand. Average = 360 ÷ 6 = 60 thousand.
solution.why_others_wrong: 72,000 divides by 5; 54,000 is February's figure; 63,500 is the average of the highest and lowest bars ((85 + 42) ÷ 2).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The mill paid the same price per bale from October to December 2025, and a price 12% higher from January to March 2026. By what percentage did its spending on bales in January–March differ from that in October–December (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Spending ∝ bales × price; compare 165 × 1.12 with 195 × 1
solution.explanation: Oct–Dec: 42 + 68 + 85 = 195 thousand bales. Jan–Mar: 72 + 54 + 39 = 165 thousand. Spending ratio = 165 × 1.12 ÷ 195 = 184.8 ÷ 195 = 0.9477, i.e. 5.23% less.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.38% less ignores the price rise; 3.38% less subtracts 12 from 15.38 instead of multiplying; 32.36% more compares 195 × 1.12 with 165, reversing the periods.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which month was the percentage fall in arrivals, compared with the previous month, the largest?

solution.concept: Compare each fall as a percentage of the previous month, not in thousands
solution.explanation: January: 13 on 85 = 15.29%. February: 18 on 72 = 25%. March: 15 on 54 = 27.78%. March has the largest percentage fall, although February has the largest fall in thousands.
solution.why_others_wrong: February has the largest fall in thousands (18) but a smaller percentage; January's fall is only 15.29%; October has no previous month in the chart.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the ratio of the rice packets sent to Indore and Ujjain together to the atta packets sent to Bhopal and Gwalior together?

solution.concept: Pick the right bar for each city before adding
solution.explanation: Rice to Indore and Ujjain = 240 + 180 = 420 thousand. Atta to Bhopal and Gwalior = 305 + 225 = 530 thousand. Ratio = 420 : 530 = 42 : 53.
solution.why_others_wrong: 53 : 42 reverses the ratio; 102 : 107 uses Ujjain's atta bar instead of its rice bar; 28 : 39 uses the rice bars of Bhopal and Gwalior (420 : 585) instead of their atta bars.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: For which city did rice packets make up the largest share of all the packets sent to it?

solution.concept: Share = rice ÷ (rice + atta) for each city
solution.explanation: Indore 240/600 = 40%; Bhopal 310/615 = 50.4%; Ujjain 180/450 = 40%; Gwalior 275/500 = 55%. Gwalior has the largest share.
solution.why_others_wrong: Bhopal received the most rice packets (310 thousand) but also many atta packets; Indore and Ujjain are at 40% each.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Each rice packet weighs 5 kg and each atta packet 10 kg. What total weight of packets did the mill send to Bhopal in September 2026?

solution.concept: Weight = packets × weight per packet; 1,000 kg = 1 tonne, so thousand packets × kg = tonnes
solution.explanation: Rice: 310 thousand × 5 kg = 1,550 tonnes. Atta: 305 thousand × 10 kg = 3,050 tonnes. Total = 4,600 tonnes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3,075 tonnes weighs every packet at 5 kg; 4,625 tonnes swaps the two packet weights; 6,150 tonnes weighs every packet at 10 kg.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Next month the mill raises rice dispatches to every city by 20% and cuts atta dispatches to every city by 10%. By what percentage does the total number of packets change (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Apply each change to its own total; the overall change is a weighted average
solution.explanation: Rice total = 240 + 310 + 180 + 275 = 1,005 thousand; atta total = 360 + 305 + 270 + 225 = 1,160 thousand; together 2,165. New total = 1,206 + 1,044 = 2,250. Change = 85 ÷ 2,165 = 3.93% increase.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.00% averages +20% and −10% as if the two totals were equal; 10.00% simply adds the two rates; '3.93% decrease' gets the direction wrong.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many hours did the manager spend on loan appraisal that week?

solution.concept: Hours = central angle ÷ 360 × 60, i.e. angle ÷ 6
solution.explanation: Loan appraisal: 84° ÷ 360° × 60 = 84 ÷ 6 = 14 hours.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 hours is customer meetings; 8.4 hours divides 84 by 10; 23.3 hours is 84 as a percentage of 360.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The time spent on customer meetings was what percentage more than the time spent on reports and training together?

solution.concept: Percentage more = difference ÷ the smaller quantity × 100
solution.explanation: Customer meetings: 16 hours; reports + training: 7 + 5 = 12 hours. 16 is 4 more than 12, and 4 ÷ 12 = 33⅓%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% divides the difference by 16; 133⅓% is 16 as a percentage of 12; 4% is the difference in hours.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The next week the manager again works 60 hours. He cuts his staff-review time by 25% and his report-writing time by 2 hours, and spends all the time saved on recovery visits; everything else is unchanged. What is the new central angle for recovery visits?

solution.concept: Work in hours, then convert back: angle = hours × 6
solution.explanation: Saved: 25% of 8 = 2 hours from staff review and 2 hours from reports, 4 hours in all. Recovery visits rise from 10 to 14 hours, so the angle = 14 × 6 = 84°.
solution.why_others_wrong: 72° adds only the 2 hours from reports; 64° adds the 4 hours to the angle as if they were degrees; 96° counts the reports saving twice (10 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 16 hours).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which market's revenue grew the most, in percentage terms, from 2024-25 to 2025-26?

solution.concept: Convert each share into rupees for its own year before comparing
solution.why_others_wrong: West grew 37.5%, second to South; North's share fell, though its revenue grew 16.7%; East's revenue did not change.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did the combined revenue from all markets other than South increase from 2024-25 to 2025-26?

solution.concept: Other markets = total − South in each year
solution.why_others_wrong: 25% is the growth of the whole company; 14.29% divides 60 by 420; 50% is South's own growth.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2025-26 the company earned a profit of 12% on its domestic revenue (all markets except Exports) and 20% on its export revenue. What was its total profit in 2025-26?

solution.concept: Split 2025-26 revenue into domestic (92%) and exports (8%)
solution.explanation: Exports = 8% of 600 = ₹48 crore; domestic = ₹552 crore. Profit = 12% of 552 + 20% of 48 = 66.24 + 9.60 = ₹75.84 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹72.00 crore applies 12% to all ₹600 crore; ₹96.00 crore averages the two rates (16%); ₹66.24 crore leaves out the export profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many new demat accounts were opened in January, February and March together?

solution.concept: Add the three monthly points
solution.why_others_wrong: 3,344 is the April–June total; 2,850 adds February to April; 1,980 leaves out February (840 + 1,140).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: By what percentage did the number of new accounts rise from February to March?

solution.concept: Percentage rise = rise ÷ February's value × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 33⅓% divides the rise by March's 1,140; 150% is March as a percentage of February; 38% treats the rise of 380 as a percentage of 1,000.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Compared with the month before, which month saw the steepest percentage drop in new demat accounts?

solution.concept: Only months with a fall count; compare falls as a percentage of the previous month
solution.explanation: February: 80 on 840 = 9.52%. April: 190 on 1,140 = 16.67%. June: 266 on 1,330 = 20%. The largest percentage fall was in June. (May was a rise.)
solution.why_others_wrong: April's fall is 16.67%; February's is 9.52%; May shows a rise of 40%, not a fall.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average number of new accounts opened per month over the six months?

solution.concept: Average = total of the six points ÷ 6
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,085 averages only January and May; 1,216.8 divides by 5; 950 is April's value.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In which year was the amount recovered the highest percentage of the amount disbursed in that year?

solution.concept: Recovery ratio = recovered ÷ disbursed for each year
solution.why_others_wrong: 2025 has the largest amount recovered but only 83.3% of disbursement; 2022 (86%) and 2023 (85%) are lower than 2024.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Over the five years taken together, the total amount recovered was what percentage of the total amount disbursed (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Divide the two five-year totals; do not average the yearly percentages
solution.why_others_wrong: 84.87% is the simple average of the five yearly percentages; 14.80% is the unrecovered share; 117.37% divides disbursed by recovered.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The gap between the amount disbursed and the amount recovered in a year is that year's net new lending. By what percentage did the net new lending grow from 2021 to 2025?

solution.concept: Net new lending = disbursed − recovered; compare 2025 with 2021
solution.why_others_wrong: 110% is the growth in disbursement alone (120 → 252); 42.86% divides the rise by 2025's 42; 175% is 42 as a percentage of 24.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many footwear orders were returned in October 2026?

solution.concept: Footwear orders = 3/12 of 2,400; then apply the 12% return rate
solution.explanation: Footwear orders = 3/12 × 2,400 = 600. Returned = 12% of 600 = 72.
solution.why_others_wrong: 528 is the footwear orders kept; 108 applies apparel's 18% to footwear; 40 is the accessories returned.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of all the orders received in October were returned (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Count the returns in each category, add, and divide by 2,400
solution.explanation: Returns: apparel 18% of 1,000 = 180; footwear 72; accessories 5% of 800 = 40. Total = 292 of 2,400 = 12.17%.
