solution.why_others_wrong: 11.67% is the simple average of the three return rates; 87.83% is the share kept; 13.11% is the share of order value returned, not of orders.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the total value of the apparel orders that were not returned?

solution.concept: Apparel kept = 82% of 1,000 orders, each worth ₹800
solution.explanation: Apparel orders = 1,000; 180 were returned, so 820 were kept. Value = 820 × 800 = ₹6,56,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹8,00,000 includes the returned orders; ₹5,57,600 also deducts the 15% commission; ₹1,44,000 is the value returned.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How much did the seller finally receive for the footwear orders, after the marketplace's commission and the reverse-shipping charges?

solution.concept: Payout = 85% of the value of orders kept − ₹60 × orders returned
solution.explanation: Footwear kept = 600 − 72 = 528, worth 528 × 1,500 = ₹7,92,000. After 15% commission: ₹6,73,200. Less reverse shipping 72 × 60 = ₹4,320: ₹6,68,880.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹6,73,200 forgets the reverse-shipping charges; ₹7,87,680 forgets the commission; ₹7,65,000 charges the commission on all 600 orders and ignores returns.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If the return rate for apparel had been 10% instead of 18%, with everything else the same, by how much would the seller's net amount for October (the marketplace's payout minus the reverse-shipping charges) have been higher?

solution.concept: 80 fewer returns: each one adds 85% of ₹800 to the payout and saves ₹60 of reverse shipping
solution.explanation: Returns fall from 180 to 100, so 80 more apparel orders are kept. Extra payout = 80 × 800 × 0.85 = ₹54,400, and 80 × ₹60 = ₹4,800 less reverse shipping. Total gain = ₹59,200.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹54,400 forgets the saved reverse shipping; ₹64,000 forgets the commission; ₹49,600 subtracts the shipping saving instead of adding it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of the total value of all orders received was returned (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Weight each category's returns by its order value
solution.why_others_wrong: 12.17% is the share of orders (by number) returned; 11.67% averages the three rates; 14.06% divides by 2,400 orders at ₹800 each, as if every order were apparel.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What percentage of all the home-loan applications received in October were approved (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Count the approvals in each segment; do not average the three percentages
solution.why_others_wrong: 70.00% is the simple average of 80%, 70% and 60%; 26.67% is the share not approved; 75.00% averages only the first two segments.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Which segment earned the branch the most processing-fee income in October?

options.text: Affordable and Mid earned the same

solution.concept: Fee income = approvals × average loan × fee rate
solution.explanation: Affordable: 72 × 22 = 1,584 lakh × 0.5% = ₹7.92 lakh. Mid: 42 × 48 = 2,016 lakh × 0.4% = ₹8.064 lakh. Premium: 18 × 110 = 1,980 lakh × 0.25% = ₹4.95 lakh. Mid is the highest.
solution.why_others_wrong: Affordable has the highest fee rate and most approvals but earns ₹7.92 lakh, slightly less; Premium has the largest loans but the lowest rate and fewest approvals; the two top segments differ by ₹14,400.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What was the average loan amount per approved application, taking all three segments together (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Average = total amount approved ÷ number of approvals
solution.explanation: Total approved = 1,584 + 2,016 + 1,980 = 5,580 lakh over 132 approvals. Average = 5,580 ÷ 132 = ₹42.27 lakh.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹60.00 lakh is the simple average of the three segment averages; ₹31.00 lakh divides by all 180 applications; ₹48.00 lakh is the Mid segment's average.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What total processing fee did the branch earn on the loans approved in October?

solution.concept: Fee = loan amount × fee rate, segment by segment
solution.explanation: Affordable 1,584 lakh × 0.5% = 7.92 lakh; Mid 2,016 lakh × 0.4% = 8.064 lakh; Premium 1,980 lakh × 0.25% = 4.95 lakh. Total = 20.934 lakh = ₹20,93,400.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹22,32,000 applies 0.4% to the whole ₹5,580 lakh; ₹15,98,400 leaves out the Premium segment's fee; ₹25,88,400 charges 0.5% on Premium loans too.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Suppose the approval rate rises to 70% in the Premium segment and falls to 70% in the Affordable segment, with the same applications and average loans, and the Mid segment unchanged. How would the total loan amount approved change?

solution.concept: Work out the change in approvals in each segment and multiply by that segment's average loan
solution.explanation: Premium: 70% of 30 = 21, which is 3 more approvals × ₹110 lakh = +₹330 lakh. Affordable: 70% of 90 = 63, which is 9 fewer × ₹22 lakh = −₹198 lakh. Net change = +₹132 lakh = +₹1.32 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rise by ₹3.30 crore' counts only the Premium gain; 'fall by ₹1.98 crore' counts only the Affordable loss; 'no change' assumes the two rate changes cancel because both move to 70%.
solution.final_answer: Option B: It would rise by ₹1.32 crore

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the utilisation of warehouse W3?

solution.concept: Utilisation = stock ÷ capacity × 100
solution.why_others_wrong: 16% is the free space as a percentage; 119.05% divides capacity by stock; 8.4% slips a decimal place.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the storage capacity of warehouse W2?

solution.concept: Capacity = stock ÷ utilisation
solution.explanation: Stock 450 tonnes is 75% of capacity, so capacity = 450 ÷ 0.75 = 600 tonnes (free space 150 tonnes).
solution.why_others_wrong: 337.5 tonnes takes 75% of the stock; 562.5 tonnes adds 25% of the stock to it; 525 tonnes adds 75 to 450.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many tonnes of stock does warehouse W4 hold?

solution.concept: Free space is the unused (100 − 76)% = 24% of capacity
solution.explanation: Free space 288 tonnes = 24% of capacity, so capacity = 288 ÷ 0.24 = 1,200 tonnes. Stock = 1,200 − 288 = 912 tonnes (76% of 1,200).
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,200 tonnes is the capacity, not the stock; 378.95 tonnes treats 288 as 76% of the capacity; 218.88 tonnes takes 76% of the free space.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Taking the five warehouses together, what is the overall utilisation (correct to two decimal places)?

solution.concept: Fill in every missing capacity and stock first; then divide the totals
steps: W1 stock 520; W2 capacity 600; W4: 1,200 and 912; W5 stock 555
solution.why_others_wrong: 74.80% is the simple average of the five utilisation percentages; 24.67% is the free share; 76.00% is W4's utilisation only.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The number of prime numbers between 50 and 80
Quantity II: The number of positive factors of 36

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: List the primes; count factors from the prime factorisation 36 = 2² × 3²
solution.explanation: Primes between 50 and 80: 53, 59, 61, 67, 71, 73, 79, so Quantity I = 7. Factors of 36: (2 + 1)(2 + 1) = 9, so Quantity II = 9. Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I > II' and 'I ≥ II' come from counting 51, 57 or 77 as primes (they are 3 × 17, 3 × 19 and 7 × 11) or from missing factors of 36.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The discount percentage equivalent to the offer 'buy 4, get 1 free'
Quantity II: The profit percentage when the cost price of 7 articles equals the selling price of 6 articles

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Buy 4 get 1 free: pay for 4, receive 5. CP of 7 = SP of 6: profit = 1 article on 6
solution.explanation: Quantity I: the buyer pays for 4 of 5 items, a discount of 1/5 = 20%. Quantity II: SP of 6 = CP of 7, so profit = 1/6 = 16⅔%. Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I < II' and 'I ≤ II' take the free item as 25% of 4 bought (1/4) for Quantity I, or the profit as 1/6 of 7.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: A two-digit number whose digits add up to 9 and differ by 3
Quantity II: 50

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Find every number that fits the description before comparing
solution.explanation: Digits a + b = 9 and a − b = ±3 give the digit pairs (6, 3) and (3, 6), so Quantity I is 63 or 36. 63 > 50 but 36 < 50, so no single relation holds.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I > II' and 'I ≥ II' consider only 63; 'I < II' and 'I ≤ II' consider only 36.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: The probability that a card drawn at random from a pack of 52 is a red card or a king
Quantity II: The probability of getting at least one six when a fair die is rolled twice

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(both); P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)
solution.explanation: Quantity I: 26 red cards + 4 kings − 2 red kings = 28 cards, so 28/52 = 7/13 ≈ 0.538. Quantity II: 1 − (5/6)² = 11/36 ≈ 0.306. Quantity I > Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I < II' and 'I ≤ II' would need Quantity II to exceed 0.538, e.g. by taking 'at least one six' as 1/6 + 1/6 + … rather than 11/36.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Quantity I > Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Compare the two quantities and choose the correct option.
Quantity I: Area (cm²) of the largest circle that can be drawn inside a square of side 14 cm (take π = 22/7)
Quantity II: Area (cm²) of the largest square that can be drawn inside a circle of radius 9 cm

options.text: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: The circle in a square has diameter = side; the square in a circle has diagonal = diameter, so area = d²/2
solution.explanation: Quantity I: radius 7 cm, area = 22/7 × 49 = 154 cm². Quantity II: the square's diagonal is 18 cm, so its area = 18²/2 = 162 cm². Quantity I < Quantity II.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I > II' and 'I ≥ II' come from taking the square's side as 9 cm (area 81) or as 18 cm (area 324 compared the other way), instead of using the diagonal.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Quantity I < Quantity II

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the area of the rhombus?
I. Its diagonals are 16 cm and 12 cm long.
II. Each of its sides is 10 cm long.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are needed

solution.concept: Area of a rhombus = ½ × product of the diagonals; a side alone does not fix the shape
solution.explanation: I alone: area = ½ × 16 × 12 = 96 cm². II alone: a rhombus of side 10 cm can be squashed into many shapes (for example diagonals 16 and 12 give 96 cm², diagonals 19.2 and 5.6 give 53.76 cm²), so II is not sufficient.
steps: II: side 10 fits many pairs of diagonals
solution.why_others_wrong: 'II alone' assumes a fixed shape for a given side; 'either' wrongly accepts II; 'both needed' overlooks that I alone already gives the area.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements. Decide which statements are sufficient to answer it.
Question: What is the speed of the train?
I. The train passes a signal pole in 15 seconds.
II. The train passes a 300 m long platform in 27 seconds.
III. The train is more than 300 m long.

options.text: Any two of the three statements together are sufficient
Only I and II together are sufficient
Only I and III together are sufficient
All three statements together are necessary

solution.concept: Two crossing times with a known platform length fix the speed; an inequality on the length does not
solution.explanation: I + II: L = 15v and L + 300 = 27v ⇒ 12v = 300 ⇒ v = 25 m/s (90 km/h), L = 375 m. I + III: L = 15v with L > 300 allows many speeds. II + III: L + 300 = 27v with L > 300 also allows many (e.g. L = 375, v = 25 or L = 1,050, v = 50).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Any two' wrongly accepts I + III and II + III; 'only I and III' gives only a range; 'all three' is more than needed, since III adds nothing to I + II.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only I and II together are sufficient

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.
Question: What is the sum of money?
I. At 10% per annum, the compound interest (compounded annually) on it for 2 years exceeds the simple interest on it for 2 years by ₹50.
II. The simple interest on it for 3 years at 10% per annum is ₹1,500.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Both statements I and II together are needed

solution.concept: For 2 years, CI − SI = P × r²; SI = P × r × t
solution.explanation: I alone: P × (0.1)² = 50 ⇒ P = ₹5,000. II alone: P × 0.1 × 3 = 1,500 ⇒ P = ₹5,000. Each statement alone gives the sum.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'I alone' and 'II alone' each overlook that the other statement also fixes P; 'both needed' assumes the rate must be found first, but both statements state it.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
